evals.prompt: I'm Priya, RevOps manager at Hartwell Logistics Cloud - B2B SaaS, around 180 people. I want a proper list of things to read and listen to so I stop finding out about stuff six months late. Realistically I have about 75 minutes a week at my desk, plus a 25-minute train commute each way that I currently waste staring out the window. Finance has frozen anything paid this year, so no memberships and no conference tickets. I want broad coverage rather than going deep on one topic. Vendor blogs are fine by me as long as I know which ones they are. Our whole stack sits on one big CRM platform. Put the list together for me.
evals.expected_output: A date-stamped watch list grouped by consumption rhythm, sized to 75 minutes/week with commute audio discounted, paid sources deleted with the reason named, a community slot reserved, a bench, and closing totals.
expectations: The list is grouped by consumption rhythm (weekly core, monthly, annual events, bench, dropped), not grouped by medium.
A 'Dropped' section names at least one paid source removed, with 'no budget / cannot expense' given as the reason.
No paid-membership community appears in the weekly, monthly, annual, or bench sections.
The attention cost of the commute podcast is halved or otherwise reduced because it rides on time already spent.
Total estimated weekly minutes is stated and is at or under 75.
Roughly 10% of the budget is explicitly reserved for one community, with source discovery or list renewal named as the reason.
A bench section names 2-3 verified substitutes instead of adding them to the main list.
Every entry carries a verification status and a date.
Every entry carries a URL.
Vendor-run entries carry an explicit vendor-run flag.
Closing totals state estimated weekly minutes against budget, counts per section, and how many entries are verified-active.
The response does not ask for a delivery date or deadline for the watch list.

evals.prompt: Give me the RevOps podcast shortlist. I listen while running, so three or four shows maximum, and I want ones that are actually still publishing - last time I subscribed to a batch off somebody's blog post and half of them hadn't shipped an episode in over a year. I'm a sales ops lead at Kestrel Freight Systems.
evals.expected_output: A short podcast list where every recommendation carries the date of its most recent confirmed episode, dormant well-known shows are excluded or flagged, and running time is treated as attention already spent.
expectations: RevOps FM is not presented as an actively publishing weekly show.
If RevOps FM appears at all, it is labelled stale or dormant with its months-silent gap stated.
The Revenue Formula is not presented as an actively publishing weekly show.
Ops Cast is either absent or flagged as ended, and is never recommended as active.
The response states that a homepage's own cadence claim such as 'weekly' does not verify a show is alive, and that only a dated episode does.
At least one show is recommended on the evidence of a recent dated episode, and RevOpsAF appears among the active recommendations.
Each recommended show carries the date of its most recent confirmed episode, not just a bare 'active' label.
The attention cost of the podcasts is halved or reduced because they ride on running time already spent.
No download, listener, or subscriber figure is invented; sources publishing no figure are recorded as 'not stated'.
No show is attributed to Sales Assembly under the name 'B2B Revenue Vitals'.
A URL is given for every recommended show.
The verification date behind the statuses is stated.

evals.prompt: I'm cleaning out a bookmarks folder I built about two years ago for revenue ops reading. Here's what I've got and what happens when I click each one: (1) opsstars.com lands on a page saying the domain is for sale; (2) saleshacker.com redirects to gtmnow.com; (3) salesforceben.com returns a 403 through my work proxy, though I'm told it's a big site; (4) seanlane.substack.com shows a 'coming soon' page with nothing published; (5) an old marketing-ops blog URL now loads a dentist practice website; (6) wizardsofops.com gives me a 'server not found' error. Tell me what to keep and what to bin. I'm ops manager at Brightside Analytics.
evals.expected_output: A per-URL triage that distinguishes genuinely dead, renamed-but-alive, resold domain, not-yet-alive, DNS-dead, and blocked-therefore-unverified, rather than a binary alive/dead split.
expectations: opsstars.com is classified as genuinely dead on the evidence of a parked or for-sale page, and is removed.
saleshacker.com redirecting to gtmnow.com is classified as renamed or merged but alive, the URL is updated, and the source is kept.
salesforceben.com is not classified as dead; the 403 is classified as unverified with the block recorded as the reason.
A manual or alternate check is recommended for the 403'd source rather than dropping it.
seanlane.substack.com is classified as not-yet-alive (live page, zero published items), excluded from the list, and noted for the next refresh.
The URL now serving a dentist practice is classified as a resold or squatted domain, distinct from the source itself being dead.
The response states that a link resolving is not evidence the source is alive, and that page content must be confirmed to match the source's subject.
The DNS resolution failure is classified as dead, and DNS failure is described as a stronger dead signal than a parked page.
At least four distinct verdicts are used across the six URLs, rather than a binary alive/dead split.
No entry is presented as verified-active without a dated item behind it.
GTMnow is named as the successor brand to Sales Hacker.
The response advises re-resolving every URL at the next refresh, including ones that worked this time.
No replacement URL is constructed from memory for any source that cannot be confirmed.

evals.prompt: Rank these five by authority so I know where to start: Growth Unhinged (85k readers), GTMnow (60k members), RevOps Impact Newsletter (6.1k subscribers), CRM Daily, and The Signal (10k subscribers). I'm a RevOps IC at Vantage Freight Group and I have maybe 20 minutes a week, so I only want the top two.
evals.expected_output: Two picks ranked on role fit and durability signals, with subscriber count explicitly rejected as the ranking basis, no invented figure for the source that publishes none, and the rest benched.
expectations: Subscriber or reader count is explicitly rejected as the basis for the ranking.
The response states that audience size measures reach, not authority.
Cross-surface recurrence, a named accountable author, and/or institutional backing are named as the durability signals used instead.
CRM Daily is not assigned an invented subscriber figure; it is recorded as 'not stated' or equivalent.
CRM Daily is flagged as agency-run rather than presented as an independent publication.
RevOps Impact Newsletter is attributed to its named practitioner author (Jeff Ignacio) rather than presented as vendor-run.
Fit to the user's IC role is applied as a ranking criterion ahead of reach.
Exactly two sources are recommended, matching the stated 20-minute budget.
The two picks are costed in minutes and totalled against the 20-minute budget.
The 85,000-reader figure is not given as the reason to read Growth Unhinged first.
Each pick carries a URL and a verification status.
One to three of the unpicked sources are named as bench substitutes rather than silently dropped.

About 45 minutes a week, and I read - I don't do podcasts.

The response states that no dedicated B2C or DTC 'RevOps' branch exists, without implying parity with the B2B side.
No B2C-specific RevOps podcast, newsletter, or community is invented to fill the gap.
Medium-agnostic frameworks such as funnel math, forecasting, or data hygiene are kept from B2B sources, with a reason given for why they still transfer.
The community and benchmark need is routed to an ecommerce operator community rather than a B2B RevOps community.
The response warns that most named benchmarks and playbooks in the B2B sources assume B2B sales cycles.
The list contains no podcast entries, matching the stated exclusion.
Audio sources are named in a 'Dropped' section with 'no podcasts' as the reason, rather than being ranked lower in the main list.
Total estimated weekly minutes is stated and is at or under 45.
Roughly 10% of the budget is reserved for one community.
Every entry carries a URL and a verification status with a date.
The list is grouped by consumption rhythm, not by medium.

evals.expected_output: A depth-oriented list of 3-5 concentrated sources plus the people publishing on those themes, with long-form deliberately promoted against the efficiency order and the reason stated.
expectations: The efficiency ordering across mediums is stated explicitly rather than left implied by row order.
The response states that long-form (podcasts, talks, events, communities) tops the value axis while sitting at or below the bottom of the efficiency axis.
Long-form is promoted against the pure efficiency order, with 'new to the field' and/or 'depth' named as the condition that justifies the promotion.
The delivered list is not composed only of newsletters and blogs.
The budget is concentrated on roughly 3-5 sources rather than spread across every medium, matching the depth answer.
People who publish on the user's named themes (revenue architecture, forecasting) are included alongside the publications.

Revenue Architecture by Jacco van der Kooij, or an equivalent foundational text, is named as the source of the frameworks rather than a blog post about them.
If any event is included, it is costed as days cleared in one block rather than as an amortised weekly minute figure.
Attention costs are given as orders of magnitude (minutes, tens of minutes, most of an hour, days) rather than as false-precision figures.
Total estimated weekly minutes is stated against the two-hour budget.
Roughly 10% of the budget is reserved for one community.
Every entry carries a URL and a verification status.

evals.prompt: Which revenue ops conferences are worth going to next year? My employer gives me a $3,500 training budget and roughly three days out of the office. I'm director of RevOps at Calder Health Systems, based in Chicago.
evals.expected_output: A short event shortlist costed as cleared days rather than amortised weekly minutes, with dead and unconfirmed events excluded or flagged and the employer budget factored into the ranking.
expectations: Events are costed as days cleared in one block, never as an amortised per-week minute figure.
The response states explicitly that amortising a multi-day conference across 52 weeks understates a cost the user pays as cleared days.
OpsStars is not recommended.
REVOLT's next edition is flagged as unconfirmed rather than assumed to recur annually.
If GTM2026 is recommended, attendgtm.com is given as the URL rather than a joinpavilion.com path.
HubSpot's event is referred to as UNBOUND and identified as the rebrand of INBOUND rather than as a separate event.
Candidate events are ranked by fit to a director-level attendee, not by attendee count or event size.
The response notes that the employer-funded budget changes the ranking by removing price as a reason to skip an event.
Dates, location, and a verification status are given for each recommended event.
The speaker roster is named as a by-product worth harvesting for who to follow.
No date is invented for any event whose next edition is unannounced.
No more events are recommended than the stated three-day allowance permits.

evals.expected_output: A people list ranked by cross-surface recurrence rather than follower count, with affiliation flagged, Chris Walker's changed focus called out, and the highest-yield surfaces for finding more people named.

The response states explicitly that follower count measures reach, not authority.
Chris Walker's current feed is flagged as no longer RevOps commentary, and he is recommended for back-catalog credibility only rather than as an active-feed follow.
The response states that LinkedIn, not X/Twitter, is where RevOps practitioners actually publish.

Rosalyn Santa Elena, or another practitioner justified by recurrence across independent surfaces, is recommended with the recurring surfaces named.

Podcast guest lists and conference speaker rosters are named as the highest-yield surfaces for finding more people.
Community team pages are ranked below guest lists and speaker rosters, and vendor benchmark posts are ranked last.
Each person is matched to a specific 'best followed for' line rather than a generic endorsement.

evals.prompt: Three months ago you built me a RevOps watch list - 6 weekly sources, 2 monthly, 1 conference, and 3 on the bench. Since then: I've read the two newsletters religiously, I listen to one of the podcasts every week, I never once opened the Slack community, and I genuinely forgot the other three existed. Also, my new employer will now pay for a peer community, which I couldn't afford before. Run the refresh. Still 90 minutes a week. I'm at Merrow Analytics now.
evals.expected_output: A refresh pass that re-resolves every URL, drops the unread entries, re-offers the previously deleted paid community because the constraint lifted, sources a discovery, re-totals against budget, and reports the failed measurement check.
expectations: Every URL is re-resolved, including the ones that worked at the last check, with renames and domain resale named as the reason.
The freshness check is re-run on every entry and newly stale entries are downgraded.
Previously unverified and not-yet-alive entries are retried rather than left at their old status.

The user's consumption report is used as an explicit refresh input, or the question of what was actually consumed is asked.
The paid peer community is re-offered specifically because the user says the budget constraint has lifted.
The response states that a source deleted for a constraint is only re-offered once the user says that constraint has lifted.
The anchor community or the newest additions are asked for one candidate discovery to verify and consider.
Estimated weekly minutes is re-totalled against the 90-minute budget and any overflow is trimmed.
A bench entry is considered for promotion onto the main list where a slot opened.
The next refresh is set or confirmed at a quarterly interval.
No source previously dropped for a constraint still in force is silently re-added.
The two-thirds consumption check is reported as failing (3 of 9 listed entries consumed), and the list is revised rather than re-presented unchanged.

evals.prompt: Can you set me up with a RevOps reading list? I'm at Halverson Grid, been in ops about four years.

Questions are asked one at a time, waiting for each answer, rather than presented as a single block.
The weekly time budget available for staying current is asked.
Whether the user is catching up before a specific moment or building a standing weekly habit is asked.
Which mediums the user actually consumes is asked, capped at two.
What is ruled out entirely (no commute time, a paywall, an unaffordable community or conference) is asked.
Breadth versus depth is asked, with a depth answer prompted to name its themes.
The segment (B2B SaaS, B2C/ecommerce, or both) is asked.
Whether vendor-run sources should be included is asked.
Whether the stack is anchored on a dominant CRM platform whose ecosystem sources should be included is asked.
No delivery date or deadline for the watch list is requested.

evals.expected_output: A list cut to the 30-minute budget with the stated ranking order, strong leftovers benched, the 'I'll find more time' premise declined, and expansion offered only on a raised budget.
expectations: The list is sized to the stated 30-minute budget rather than delivered as the full inventory.
The response states that a list overrunning its budget gets abandoned, and that abandonment is total failure rather than partial.
The 'I'll find more time' premise is declined as a reason to overstuff, and the stated budget is held.
Strong leftovers are placed on a bench of 2-3 named substitutes rather than in the main list.
The ranking order is stated out loud rather than left implied by row order.
The output is not a flat unranked list topped by a 'start here' pick justified by size or fame.
Roughly 10% of the 30-minute budget is reserved for one community.
Every entry carries a verification status and date, and no entry is presented as verified when it is not.
Estimated weekly minutes is totalled against the 30-minute budget.
Attention is sized as orders of magnitude rather than as precise per-source figures.
Expanding the list is offered only if the user raises the stated budget, rather than done unilaterally.
